title: B1.2 Lesson 4: AHL Proteins: Arrangement, Quaternary Structure, Collagen and Insulin

q.1(a): 1(a). State what determines whether an amino acid is hydrophobic or hydrophilic.
q.1(b): 1(b). Predict where the hydrophobic amino acids of a protein will end up if the protein sits in the middle of a phospholipid bilayer. Give a reason.

q.2(a): 2(a). Discuss the arrangement of hydrophobic and hydrophilic amino acids in a protein dissolved in the cytoplasm.
q.2(b): 2(b). Explain how that arrangement makes the protein soluble.
q.2(c): 2(c). Suggest why such proteins are described as globular rather than fibrous.

q.3(a): 3(a). Discuss the arrangement of amino acids in an integral membrane protein.
q.3(b): 3(b). Explain why this arrangement means the protein cannot flip over in the membrane.
q.4(a): 4(a). Discuss the arrangement of amino acids in a channel protein.
q.4(b): 4(b). Explain how this arrangement allows ions to cross a membrane that they could not otherwise cross.

q.5(a): 5(a). Describe the quaternary structure of a protein.
q.5(b): 5(b). State the types of interaction that hold the subunits together.
q.5(c): 5(c). Explain why lysozyme, a single polypeptide, is said to have no quaternary structure.
q.6(a): 6(a). Compare the structure of conjugated and non-conjugated proteins.
q.6(b): 6(b). State one example of a conjugated protein and one example of a non-conjugated protein, naming the prosthetic group where there is one.
q.6(c): 6(c). Suggest why haemoglobin could not transport oxygen if its prosthetic groups were removed.

q.7(b): 7(b). Explain why glycine must occupy every third position in the chain.
q.7(c): 7(c). State one function of collagen in the body and relate it to its tensile strength.
q.8(a): 8(a). Describe the structure of an insulin molecule.
